## Chapter Summary

Monitoring runs audit tests every period on new data and keeps the results over time. Continuous auditing is internal audit's ongoing, technology-based assessment of risks and controls; continuous monitoring is management's ongoing review of its own controls, on which continuous auditing depends. Rule tests produce exceptions, records that fail a deterministic rule, while analytical tests produce anomalies, records or periods that differ from what is expected and call for a closer look. A monitoring system must keep its exceptions reviewable, through tests that state their rule, population, frequency, and expected result, and its results belong to the people who oversee the controls rather than to the people whose transactions it tests.

An exception register holds the exceptions of every test in one table, one row per exception per test, with the same columns whatever the process. In Power BI it is built in Power Query: each test becomes a flag column, unpivoting turns the flags into rows from which the exceptions are kept, and appending stacks the exceptions of several processes, the counterpart of Chapter 12's UNION ALL, matching columns by name rather than position. Tutorial 16.1 rebuilt Chapter 8's journal entry tests and risk scores, drilled from the highest-scoring entry to its ledger lines, and reconciled the population of entries to the ledger. Tutorial 16.2 added the purchasing and payroll tests of Chapter 12 and Exercise 12.5, appended the register, and measured each test's exceptions against its population.

The monitoring page shows exceptions by test and month as a heat map, with the number in every cell, and leads by drill-through to the documents behind a cell. Charles River's register showed two patterns: most journal entry and purchase order exceptions cluster in the first month of every year, which points to how the controls operate at that time, and one test, registers approved by the employee they pay, recurs every month, which points to the design of the control. Rates per thousand documents show whether a process improves as its volume changes, which counts alone hide.

Each exception needs a disposition. Kept in a table of their own and merged into the register on the test and the document, the dispositions survive every refresh, and the exceptions without one are the open exceptions, the reviewer's work for the month. A test that the dispositions match their exceptions catches mistyped keys. Reviewers start with documents that fail several tests and with exceptions that are new, record an expected exception once, and report an exception that recurs by design as one finding on the control. The concentration of approval is measured on the population, as the share of each process's documents that each employee approved.

A report is evidence only if its populations are complete, its calculations correct, its data current, and its changes controlled. Tutorial 16.3 tested the purchase orders for gaps and the registers for payments, stated the date through which every population runs, which for payroll stops before the year ends, and reran the package's tests as audit evidence without changing the package. Saving a report as a Power BI project lets version control record and compare every change, while a copy of a .pbix file escapes every control. How reports are published, secured, and shared is covered in [the appendix on publishing and security](#sec-appendix-publishing).
